analysis.one_liner: Redirects COVID school relief money and federal tax credits into private school scholarships.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on August 25, 2020 with three cosponsors and never received a committee hearing, markup, or vote in either chamber before Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have taken 10 percent of the emergency school money states received under the CARES Act and handed it to private-school scholarship organizations. It also would have created a new federal tax credit — up to $5 billion a year nationwide — for individuals and corporations that donate to those organizations. Scholarships would go to students from families earning up to 200 percent of their state's median income, or to children with disabilities, to pay private school tuition and other education expenses.
analysis.who_benefits: Families earning up to 200 percent of their state's median household income, and families of children with disabilities, could have used the scholarships for private school tuition and other elementary or secondary education expenses. Private and religious K-12 schools would have gained tuition-paying students, scholarship-granting organizations would have gained a federally funded pipeline (keeping up to 5 percent for administration and outreach), and donors would have received a dollar-for-dollar federal tax credit — up to 10 percent of adjusted gross income for individuals and 5 percent of taxable income for corporations — letting them redirect tax they would otherwise owe.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families seeking private schooling; private schools and donors

how_it_helps.text: States would have been required to reserve 10 percent of their CARES Act education stabilization funds (the emergency COVID school funding under section 18003) and award it as subgrants to scholarship-granting organizations, with at least 95 percent of each subgrant spent on scholarships.

Scholarships would have gone to 'eligible students' — children from households earning no more than 200 percent of their state's median household income, or children with disabilities — for elementary and secondary education expenses recognized by the state, including private school attendance.

Individuals would have received a tax credit equal to their full contribution (capped at 10 percent of adjusted gross income, with a five-year carryforward), and corporations a credit capped at 5 percent of taxable income, with a national limit of $5 billion in credited contributions per fiscal year.

The Treasury Department, working with the Education Department, would have run a web portal listing eligible scholarship organizations, letting donors contribute and instantly obtain pre-approval of their tax credit, with $50 million appropriated to run it.

analysis.who_pays: Public school systems, which would have lost 10 percent of their emergency COVID relief funds. The federal Treasury, which would have forgiven up to $5 billion a year in tax revenue through the donation credit. And, in states with existing tax-credit scholarship programs, at least half of each state's relief carve-out would have been distributed in proportion to 2019 contributions — directing money to organizations that were already operating.
analysis.who_pays_short: Public schools and the federal Treasury

drawbacks.text: States would have had to divert 10 percent of their CARES Act emergency education funds to private school scholarships, reducing the relief available to the public school systems serving nearly all students during the pandemic.

Because the credit equals the full amount of a contribution, a donor's net cost would have been near zero — up to 10 percent of an individual's adjusted gross income could be redirected from federal revenue to the private school of the donor's choosing, with no income limit on the donor.

Education providers accepting scholarship funds would not have been considered recipients of federal financial assistance, and nothing in the bill could be read to allow federal control over private, religious, or home education providers — meaning funds would have flowed to private schools without the rules attached to federal aid.

In states with existing tax-credit scholarship programs, at least 50 percent of the relief carve-out would have been distributed in proportion to 2019 contributions, advantaging organizations that were already running those programs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some lower- and middle-income families would have received genuine tuition help, and that benefit was real. But the money would have come from public schools' pandemic relief and from up to $5 billion a year in forgiven federal revenue, and the private schools receiving it would have been shielded from the federal requirements that come with federal aid. The credit structure — a full dollar-for-dollar offset with no cap on the donor's income — is the core of the bill, and it works mainly as a financing channel for private education rather than as targeted student aid.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, neither ever took it up, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Bradley Byrne (R-AL) introduced the School Choice Now Act on August 25, 2020, joined by three cosponsors — one Democrat and two Republicans.
The same day, the House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, to the Education and Labor Committee.
No hearing, markup, or vote is recorded for the bill at either committee, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 without the bill receiving floor action in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public school systems kept their full CARES Act relief allocations, and the federal Treasury kept up to $5 billion a year that the donation credit would have forgiven. Supporters of private school choice gained nothing.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to two committees; no further action followed before the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of primary jurisdiction for the tax-credit title, took no recorded action on the bill before the Congress ended.

against.what_they_did: As chair of the second committee of referral, took no recorded action on the bill before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only three members cosponsored — two Republicans and one Democrat — and no vote ever occurred, so no partisan split can be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill would have created new tuition-paying customers through scholarships funded by diverted CARES relief and tax-credited donations. Some families would have gained access to private schooling while the public schools serving most children lost 10 percent of their emergency funding, and the private providers would have accepted the money free of federal-aid requirements.

The bill would have made these nonprofits the permanent channel for federal education money — 10 percent of CARES relief plus up to $5 billion a year in tax-credited donations — while allowing each to keep up to 5 percent for administration and outreach. Families would have received scholarships through them, but a private intermediary would have stood between public funding and education.

States would have been required to carve 10 percent out of their CARES Act education stabilization funds and award it to private school scholarship organizations instead. The bill died in committee, so no funds were diverted.

A full tax credit — up to 10 percent of adjusted gross income for individuals and 5 percent of taxable income for corporations — would have let donors redirect federal tax dollars to private schools of their choice at little net cost to themselves. The public would have borne the forgone revenue while donors, not any public process, chose where it went.
